Original title might be Kiss in the Furze (spelled with an e)

The oldest source seems to be from William Litton, 1800 to 1802, when he was the musician on board one of sixteen armed ships sailing to China and back. From reading the commentary regarding the transcription of William Litton, “The notes in the text are difficult to decipher because Litten’s handwriting and spelling are both very bad, and in places the paper has bled.” Because he was a musician, the musical notes were easy to read.

Definition of Furze: “A thorny evergreen shrub, with yellow flowers.”

There is an actual place, “Yellow Furze,” about 34 Km northwest of Dublin… which also happens to be in the county of Meath (east of Westmeath, the subject of the common title now).

↳ Posted by Bryce on April 26th, 2020.

The Humours Of Westmeath, X:12

Setting for mouth whistling.

After writing a good few music scores of this kind I realised that D Major is not the best key for mouth whistling. It usually requires changes of octave. And many times there is a choice of where to do them. It can also happen that it is very difficult to keep the original phrasing when doing the octave changes.

But for this particular tune it is quite clear where to do the octave changes, the tune gives you the chance to do them without having to change the phrasing much.

For the melody I took the version of this great album that is in YouTube, it is the second tune in the set:

https://youtu.be/JD53hwDmXPg

↳ Posted by Fernando Durbán Galnares on March 7th, 2021.

The Rakes Of Westmeath, X:14

From an old recording I made in some pub that I’ve forgotten of some fiddler I’ve forgotten (sorry). Thanks to the miracle of the interweb I’ve just discovered the name (although it seems quite different to the first setting). It is, of course, the C naturals in the last bar of the A and B parts that pop out and give this little toon its charm.
